topics.title: Amy: contexts, form and key sequences

items.definition: Made almost entirely from archive and home footage, Amy lets the singer seem to tell her story, and asks who failed her.
items.examples: From a teenage Amy singing “Happy Birthday” on a friend’s camcorder to her body being carried out of her Camden home.
keyFacts: No on-screen talking heads: interviewees are heard as audio only, over images of Amy
A rise-and-fall narrative structured like a tragic drama
Killer line: “Kapadia assembles digital-era archive into a tragic narrative that implicates family, management, media and the spectator in Amy Winehouse’s destruction.”
items.examTip: Every Amy answer should name a sequence and how it was made from archive material.

items.definition: A north London jazz and soul singer whose album Back to Black made her a global star; she died aged 27 in July 2011.
items.examples: Back to Black (2006) included “Rehab”; she won five Grammys in 2008.
keyFacts: Her death from alcohol poisoning came after years of addiction and bulimia
Her lyrics were autobiographical, which the film exploits
Fame arrived with the rise of camera phones and celebrity websites
items.examTip: Keep biography brief: the exam is about the FILM.

items.definition: Directed by Asif Kapadia and produced by James Gay-Rees (On the Corner), with Universal Music and Film4 involvement.
items.examples: It won the Oscar and BAFTA for Best Documentary and became one of the highest-grossing British documentaries.
keyFacts: Premiered at Cannes in 2015
Distributed by Altitude in the UK and A24 in the US
Universal Music owned much of the music, raising questions about independence
items.examTip: Institutional context matters for the debate about who controls the story.

items.definition: Kapadia’s Senna (2010) used only archive footage, no talking heads; Amy repeats and refines that method.
items.examples: He recorded around 100 audio interviews, often in darkened rooms to help people speak openly.
keyFacts: Audio-only interviews keep the screen on Amy
He trained as a fiction director: he wanted the film to feel like a drama
Editor Chris King and composer Antonio Pinto also worked on Senna
items.examTip: A clear auteur angle: Kapadia’s archive-only signature.

items.definition: Praised by critics, but Amy’s father Mitch Winehouse said the film was misleading and unfair to him.
items.examples: The film includes Amy singing “Rehab” about her dad thinking she was fine.
keyFacts: Raises the ethical question of whose version of the truth a documentary tells
Shows editing shapes blame: selection is argument
Kapadia defended the film as true to what interviewees told him
items.examTip: Use the controversy to evaluate how “real” the documentary is.

items.definition: Camcorder videos, phone clips, TV, concerts and paparazzi footage, often low resolution, form almost the whole film.
items.examples: Grainy early videos of Amy with friends feel intimate; later paparazzi images feel invasive.
keyFacts: Image quality shifts as fame grows: from private camcorder to public press
Footage was shot by others, so Kapadia constructs meaning through selection
Digital zooms and reframing enlarge tiny or blurred images
items.examTip: Identify WHO shot each kind of footage: it changes its meaning.

items.definition: Friends, family and colleagues are heard but not seen, laid over footage of Amy.
items.examples: Childhood friends Juliette Ashby and Lauren Gilbert and first manager Nick Shymansky narrate her early life.
keyFacts: No talking heads: the spectator stays “with” Amy
Voices can contradict the images, inviting active reading
Some interviews sound like confessions
items.examTip: Contrast with expository documentaries that show experts on screen.

items.definition: Amy’s handwritten lyrics appear on screen as she sings, linking songs to the life events behind them.
items.examples: Lyrics to “Back to Black” appear as the film covers her relationship with Blake Fielder-Civil.
keyFacts: Positions Amy as author of her own story
Makes the songs into evidence and narration
Creates intimacy: we read her words in her hand
items.examTip: A distinctive technique: name it in every Amy essay.

items.definition: Non-linear digital editing shapes huge amounts of archive into a chronological tragedy with rising tension.
items.examples: Paparazzi sequences are cut fast with flashes and noise; quiet home videos are given time.
keyFacts: The rhythm turns real footage into a dramatic arc
Juxtaposition implies blame without a narrator saying it
Montage of comedians mocking Amy implicates the media and the audience
items.examTip: Editing = the documentary’s argument.

items.definition: Amy’s own songs, live recordings and Antonio Pinto’s score shape emotion; paparazzi noise becomes oppressive.
items.examples: The shutter clicks and shouted name during paparazzi scenes; her voice in the studio with Tony Bennett.
keyFacts: Pinto’s score adds fiction-style emotional cues
Sound design heightens the violence of fame
Silence and Amy’s isolated voice create intimacy
items.examTip: Sound design shows documentaries are constructed, not neutral.

items.definition: A teenage Amy messes about with friends on a home camcorder and sings “Happy Birthday” in a startling jazz voice.
items.examples: Low-quality home video, natural sound, no score at first.
keyFacts: Establishes intimacy and her raw talent
The amateur image connotes innocence before fame
Sets up the tragic arc: we know how it ends
items.examTip: Pair with the ending to discuss narrative structure.

items.definition: The film links the song “Rehab” to Amy refusing rehab after her father said she did not need to go.
items.examples: Audio interviews from Nick Shymansky recall the moment; the song plays over performance footage.
keyFacts: Implies Mitch’s influence on a fatal decision
The song becomes evidence
The basis of Mitch’s objections to the film
items.examTip: Strong for representation and the ethics of selection.

items.definition: Amy is surrounded by photographers; flashes white out the image and shutter noise fills the soundtrack.
items.examples: Fast cutting, strobing flashes and shouted questions as she tries to get home.
keyFacts: Form makes the spectator feel hounded
Digital cameras made constant celebrity surveillance possible
Implicates the spectator, who also consumed these images
items.examTip: Your best digital-debate evidence.

items.definition: Performing via satellite from London, Amy wins Record of the Year and looks stunned and fragile.
items.examples: Close-ups of her reaction; friends recall her saying the moment felt empty without drugs.
keyFacts: The peak of success shown as hollow
Satellite link: a digital-era image of global fame
Shifts the spectator from celebration to sorrow
items.examTip: Good for structure: triumph placed right before decline.

items.definition: In the studio for the duet “Body and Soul”, Amy is anxious and self-critical; Bennett is patient and kind.
items.examples: Observational footage in close-up; she apologises and restarts.
keyFacts: Shows her vulnerability and musicianship
A rare moment of respect from the industry
Feels like observational documentary in the Longinotto style
items.examTip: Useful when applying Longinotto.

items.definition: Amy stumbles through a 2011 concert in Belgrade and is booed; weeks later her body is carried from her home.
items.examples: Overhead press footage of the body bag; the film then returns to images of young Amy.
keyFacts: Audience mockery and media spectacle at their cruellest
The ending uses press footage: the media’s gaze to the end
Return to early footage creates a mournful circular structure
items.examTip: Strong ending evidence for any question on representation or ethics.

items.definition: Amy appears as a gifted, funny, vulnerable artist, a victim of addiction, fame and the people around her.
items.examples: Her wit in early interviews contrasts with her later exhaustion.
keyFacts: A sympathetic, possibly selective portrait
Gender: the media shamed her body, relationships and appearance
She seems the author of her story, though the edit is Kapadia’s
items.examTip: Question the representation: who constructed it?

items.definition: Juxtaposition invites the spectator to blame Mitch, Blake, management and media, and finally themselves.
items.examples: Clips of TV comedians joking about her addiction.
keyFacts: No narrator says “who is to blame”: editing implies it
Spectators who laughed at the jokes in 2008 are confronted
Different viewers (fans, family) respond very differently
items.examTip: Links the documentary to spectatorship skills from Component 1.

topics.title: Critical debate: the significance of digital technology

items.definition: Has digital technology transformed film since the 1990s, or has filmmaking changed less than it seems?
items.examples: Sample question: “How far has digital technology had an impact on your chosen documentary film?”
keyFacts: One side: digital transforms production, editing, distribution and the relationship with reality
Other side: narrative forms and documentary ethics have changed very little
The spec frames it as “a developing debate”
items.examTip: Always argue both sides, then judge “how far”.

items.definition: Cheap camcorders, phones and digital press cameras meant Amy’s life was filmed constantly.
items.examples: Home videos, mobile clips and paparazzi footage make up most of the film.
keyFacts: Amy could not exist in this form before digital recording
Fame in the digital age = permanent surveillance
Much of the footage was shot by amateurs, not filmmakers
items.examTip: Strongest argument that digital had a very significant impact.

items.definition: Digital editing let the team search, reorder and reshape vast archive material quickly.
items.examples: Low-resolution clips are reframed, stabilised and graded to sit together.
keyFacts: Makes archive-only feature documentaries practical
Digital manipulation raises questions of authenticity
Audio interviews are layered freely over images
items.examTip: Name “non-linear editing” precisely: the sample question does.

items.definition: Online clips shaped Amy’s fame; streaming and downloads widened the documentary’s audience.
items.examples: Many viewers first knew Amy through viral clips and tabloid websites.
keyFacts: The spectator already “knew” the images, which changes response
Documentaries now reach streaming audiences worldwide
Celebrity websites made mockery instant and global
items.examTip: Links digital debate to spectator response.

items.definition: Compilation documentaries existed long before digital, and Amy still uses a classic rise-and-fall narrative.
items.examples: Archive compilation goes back to Soviet filmmaker Esfir Shub in the 1920s.
keyFacts: Selection and editing always shaped documentary “truth”
The tragic structure is as old as the biopic
Ethical questions about consent are not new
items.examTip: Needed for a balanced, top-band judgement.

items.definition: Watkins attacks the “monoform”: mainstream media’s fast, fragmented, single-voice style that leaves no room to think.
items.examples: His docu-dramas Culloden (1964) and The War Game (1965) used actors and reconstruction to question documentary.
keyFacts: Monoform: rapid editing, constant music, a linear story, no space for reflection
Amy critiques tabloid media, yet uses fast editing and emotive music itself
So Watkins helps judge whether Amy resists or repeats the monoform
items.examTip: Applying Watkins critically to Amy makes an excellent evaluative essay.

items.definition: Broomfield appears on screen with his boom mic and small crew, using his interview style to expose people’s real views.
items.examples: Kurt and Courtney (1998); Whitney: Can I Be Me (2017), another music documentary.
keyFacts: Calls his films a “rollercoaster ride... a diary into the future”
Crew of no more than three: minimal filmmaking presence
Amy is the opposite: Kapadia is never seen
items.examTip: Use as a contrast to show what Amy’s invisible style gains and loses.

items.definition: Longinotto stays invisible, avoids voiceover and captions, and wants films to feel like fiction without conclusions.
items.examples: Sisters in Law (2005); she does not like to zoom or pan and wants viewers to “jump into someone else’s experience”.
keyFacts: Identification with characters is central
Amy shares invisibility and fiction-like identification
But Amy uses interviews, captions, music and implied conclusions
items.examTip: Longinotto is the most natural fit for Amy: argue how far.

items.definition: Moore is a visible, committed presence who uses humour and argument to give “balance” against mainstream media.
items.examples: Bowling for Columbine (2002), Fahrenheit 9/11 (2004).
keyFacts: Participatory and performative mode
Openly takes sides
Amy is polemical in a hidden way: it argues through editing, not presence
items.examTip: Use to show Amy still makes an argument without a presenter.

items.term: John Grierson: “the creative treatment of actuality”
items.definition: Grierson’s 1930s definition: documentary shapes real material creatively; it is never a neutral record.
items.examples: Amy creatively treats real footage to tell a tragedy.
keyFacts: The founder of the British documentary movement
Selection and arrangement are always creative
A good opening definition in a documentary essay
items.examTip: Open with Grierson to frame the documentary as constructed.

items.definition: Nichols’ six modes: poetic, expository, observational, participatory, reflexive and performative.
items.examples: Amy mixes expository argument (without a narrator) with observational and poetic moments.
keyFacts: Expository: argues a case, often with voiceover
Observational: “fly on the wall”, no intervention
Participatory/performative: the filmmaker is present and involved
items.examTip: Classify Amy, then explain why it resists one mode.

items.definition: Modern documentaries blur fact and fiction; editing, music and structure shape what seems true.
items.examples: The spec: set documentaries “make the division between fact and fiction ambiguous”.
keyFacts: Consent: Amy cannot approve how she is shown
Family members disputed the film’s version
The spectator should actively question the evidence
items.examTip: Ethics adds depth to any documentary answer.
